newsitem.title: USA: Bombing trial inspired confidence system can work.
newsitem.headline: Bombing trial inspired confidence system can work.

text.p: The Oklahoma city bombing trial showed an increasingly sceptical American public the justice system can move swiftly and smoothly, especially if a no-nonsense judge is in charge.

The trial of accused bomber Timothy McVeigh prompted inevitable and favourable comparisons with another high-profile case, the murder trial of O.J. Simpson, who was acquitted in 1995 of murdering his wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman.
The televised Simpson case, with its circus-like atmosphere both inside and outside the courtroom, soured millions of Americans on their legal system.

The bombing trial ended on Monday after a jury of seven men and five women completed 23 hours of deliberations spread over four days and found that McVeigh was guilty of murder and conspiracy by blowing up the Oklahoma City federal building, the worst attack on civilians ever committed on American soil.
"It was close to being a model trial, with careful preparation on the defence and prosecution side," University of Colorado law professor Christopher Mueller said of the bombing trial.

Testimony in the emotionally and racially charged Simpson criminal trial took more than eight months and the jury, depressed and fed up by being sequestered, returned a verdict after about two hours of actual deliberations.

But the Oklahoma City bombing jurors were not sequestered for the trial of the man accused of planning and carrying out the blast in which 168 people were killed. Nor were they subjected to months of testimony and courtroom wrangling.

Testimony in the McVeigh case took only five weeks, hearing 162 witnesses -- 137 for the prosecution and 25 for the defence. Prosecutors could have presented more than 300 witnesses but chose to dump problematic ones.

"It's mind-boggling. This case was the biggest crime in U.S. history and results in a trial conducted in a little over a month," said Robert Precht, director of the Office of Public Service at the University of Michigan Law School.

Mueller said the smooth sailing of the McVeigh trial was due to three factors: the lack of television cameras, which beamed the Simpson criminal trial into millions of homes, the absence of lawyers trying to bait each other and a strict judge, Federal District Court Judge Richard Matsch.
Cameras are not allowed in federal courthouses.

"The system worked efficiently. You can have a trial not always sidetracked and full of bickering," said William Pizzi, a former federal prosecutor in New Jersey and a law professor at the University of Colorado.
Unlike the Simpson trial, there were few "sidebar" meetings at the bench between judge and attorneys, which may serve to delay a trial and alienate the jury.

In order to avoid the carnival-like atmosphere that poisoned the Simpson trial, Matsch issued a sweeping gag order that prevented the lawyers from discussing the case out of court and playing to the television cameras.

Matsch clearly had the Simpson trial on his mind and there were frequent references to it in the courtroom, where the judge even snapped at one lawyer during jury selection: "We're not trying the O.J. Simpson case."
Legal analysts gave much of the credit for the smooth running of the trial to Matsch, a hard-nosed, 66-year-old jurist who was appointed to the federal bench in 1974 by President Richard Nixon.

He kept the lawyers on their toes and the trial moving much faster than anyone had predicted after he took over the case and brought it to his court in Denver, saying McVeigh could not get a fair trial in Oklahoma City.

While he took a fatherly approach to the jurors, lawyers were not immune from his sharp tongue. In fact, Matsch has been called the "Anti-Ito," a reference to Lance Ito, the judge in the Simpson criminal trial who critics said let the case turn into a fiasco.

Another reason the bombing trial moved swiftly was that the prosecution streamlined its case in the face of criticism over charges of sloppy, pro-prosecution work at the Federal Bureau of Investigation crime laboratory. A Justice Department report in April said the crime lab provided flawed evidence in some major cases, including the Oklahoma City bombing.
"The trial would have lasted twice as long," Colorado law professor Mueller said, if the prosecution had not curtailed its case.

Prosecutors portrayed the Gulf War veteran as a right-wing fanatic, driven to carry out the bombing by his hatred for the government over the way federal agents handled a siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993.
